---
title: 'Connect your agent (MCP)'
status: preview
description: 'Let Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code and other MCP clients read builds, explain failures and run builds through Oore.'
---

Oore has an [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server built into the
daemon at `/mcp`. An agent connected to it can list your apps and builds,
explain why a build failed, read logs, start a build and wait for it, and send
a build to testers. There is nothing to install: the server is part of every
Oore instance and always matches its version.

The agent acts with an API token. It can do what the token allows and nothing
more: every tool call is an ordinary API request, with the same permission
checks and audit log entries.

## What you need

- Instance owner access, to turn the server on.
- An [API token](/team/api-tokens) for the agent.
- Your Oore address, such as `https://oore.example.com`. Below it is
  `<OORE_URL>`.

## 1. Turn on the MCP server

The server is off on a new instance, and `/mcp` answers `404` while it is off.
An instance owner opens **Settings** › **General**, and under **AI agents**
turns on **MCP server**. Other people see the switch but cannot change it.
Turning it off again cuts off every connected agent at once, and the audit log
records both changes.

## 2. Create a token for the agent

Open **Settings** › **API tokens** and create a token named for the agent,
such as `claude-code-laptop`. Give it the smallest role that covers what the
agent should do: **QA viewer** to read, **Developer** to run builds. See
[API tokens](/team/api-tokens).

Keep the token out of your repository. The examples below read it from the
`OORE_TOKEN` environment variable:

```bash
export OORE_TOKEN='<TOKEN>'
```

## 3. Connect your client

### Claude Code

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http oore <OORE_URL>/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $OORE_TOKEN"
```

To share the setup with everyone working on an app, commit `.mcp.json` at the
root of the app's repository. Claude Code fills in `${OORE_TOKEN}` from each
person's environment:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "oore": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "<OORE_URL>/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${OORE_TOKEN}" }
    }
  }
}
```

### Cursor

Add the server to `.cursor/mcp.json` in the repository, or to
`~/.cursor/mcp.json` for every project:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "oore": {
      "url": "<OORE_URL>/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${env:OORE_TOKEN}" }
    }
  }
}
```

### VS Code

Add `.vscode/mcp.json`. VS Code asks for the token once and stores it
securely:

```json
{
  "inputs": [
    {
      "type": "promptString",
      "id": "oore-token",
      "description": "Oore API token",
      "password": true
    }
  ],
  "servers": {
    "oore": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "<OORE_URL>/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${input:oore-token}" }
    }
  }
}
```

### Other clients

Any client that speaks Streamable HTTP works: the URL is `<OORE_URL>/mcp` and
every request carries `Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>`. Oore follows MCP
revision `2026-07-28` (stateless, one POST per request) and also serves
clients on older revisions.

### Clients that start a local command

Some clients can only start a program and talk to it over standard input and
output. [`oore mcp`](/reference/cli/oore-mcp) bridges that to the daemon:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "oore": {
      "command": "oore",
      "args": ["mcp"],
      "env": { "OORE_URL": "<OORE_URL>", "OORE_TOKEN": "<TOKEN>" }
    }
  }
}
```

Use `["mcp", "--read-only"]` to offer the agent only the tools that change
nothing.

## Tools

Read tools change nothing:

| Tool                           | What it does                                                             |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `list_apps`                    | Apps you can see, with IDs and platforms.                                |
| `list_pipelines`               | An app's pipelines and whether their `.oore.yaml` is usable.             |
| `list_builds`                  | Recent builds, by app, pipeline, status, branch or commit.               |
| `get_build`                    | One build with its steps, commit and store outcome.                      |
| `get_build_logs`               | Log lines, by step or search, newest last, with a size cap.              |
| `diagnose_build`               | Why a build failed: step, exit code, cause, fix, log tail, failed tests. |
| `wait_for_build`               | Waits up to about 50 seconds, then says whether to ask again.            |
| `list_artifacts`               | Files a build produced.                                                  |
| `get_install_link`             | A short-lived install link for an artifact.                              |
| `list_releases`, `get_release` | Store releases and what can be done next.                                |
| `get_store_readiness`          | Whether a pipeline can publish, and what blocks it.                      |
| `validate_pipeline_file`       | Checks the text of an `.oore.yaml`.                                      |
| `list_workflows`               | Workflows a pipeline can run at a branch or commit.                      |
| `list_tester_groups`           | Tester groups a build can be sent to.                                    |

Build tools need a role that may run builds. QA viewers do not see them:

| Tool                       | What it does                                                       |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `run_build`                | Starts a build of a pipeline, by app and pipeline name or ID.      |
| `cancel_build`             | Stops a queued or running build.                                   |
| `rerun_build`              | Builds the same commit and settings again.                         |
| `retry_step`               | Runs an earlier build again from one step, such as a store upload. |
| `set_release_notes`        | Saves an app version's release notes.                              |
| `share_build_with_testers` | Sends a build to a tester group.                                   |

Apps and pipelines can be given by name or ID. Results are kept small: builds
leave out their full configuration, and log tools say when lines were left
out and how to read more. A failed call answers with the API's error `code`,
its HTTP `status` and a `hint`.

The server also offers the [`.oore.yaml` version 2
reference](/reference/config/oore-yaml-v2) as a resource, and a **Diagnose this
build** prompt that walks the agent through `diagnose_build` and the logs.

## Verify the connection

Ask the agent "Which Oore apps can you see?". It should call `list_apps` and
name your apps. Then try "Why did the last Android build fail?".

From a terminal, the server answers a tool list with your token:

```bash
curl -sS <OORE_URL>/mcp \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OORE_TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \
  -H 'MCP-Protocol-Version: 2025-11-25' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"}'
```

## Troubleshooting

**`404 Not Found` from `/mcp`**

The MCP server is off. An instance owner turns it on in **Settings** ›
**General** › **AI agents**.

**`401` and `invalid_session`**

The token is wrong, expired or revoked. Create a new one.

**`403` and `origin_not_allowed`**

The request came from a web page on another address. Browsers may only call
`/mcp` from the Oore instance's own address. Desktop agents send no `Origin`
and are not affected.

**A tool answers `404` for an app or build you expect**

The token's owner is not a member of that app. Add them in the app's
**Members**, or use a token of someone who is.
